evidence.label: Integer multiplication below n log n

headline: A tape-based computer can multiply huge whole numbers slightly faster than the long-conjectured n log n limit.
scope: The result covers exact multiplication on a Turing machine with a fixed number of tapes. Its saving is astronomically small.
plain: Multiplying two n-bit numbers on a simple tape-based model computer was known to take about n log n steps. In 1971, Schönhage and Strassen proposed that this was the best possible growth rate. This paper claims to prove a slower-growing method, saving a factor of (log n) to the power 2^−182. If the proof holds, that conjecture fails in this model. The gain is far too small to matter in practice.
doesNot: This does not give a faster multiplication method for real computers.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Karatsuba and Ofman, first method faster than school multiplication (earliest result the paper cites)
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to break a growth rate conjectured optimal since 1971, though the gain is purely theoretical.

explanation:
Multiply 1234 by 5678 the way you learned at school. Each of the 4 top digits meets each of the 4 bottom digits. That makes 16 small products, which add up to 7,006,652. Double the length of both numbers, and the work roughly quadruples. Computers multiply in bits (binary digits, 0 or 1). Take two numbers that are each 2^20 bits long, about a million bits. The school method then needs about 1.1 trillion small products.

Faster methods have a long history. In 1962, Karatsuba and Ofman found a trick that beats the school method. It splits each number in half and applies the same trick again to the smaller pieces. In 1971, Schönhage and Strassen proved a much faster bound. Their time grows like n log n log log n, where n is the number of bits. Here log n is the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1. For a million bits, log n is about 20. So n log n is about 21 million, against 1.1 trillion for the school method.

Schönhage and Strassen also proposed n log n as the best possible growth rate. Fürer narrowed the gap in 2007. Harvey and van der Hoeven then proved a bound of order n log n, in a paper published in 2021. That met the conjectured limit. The open question was whether anyone could go below it.

The answer depends on the machine you count steps on. All of these bounds use a multitape Turing machine. That is a simple model computer. It reads and writes symbols on a fixed number of long tapes, moving one cell at a time. In other models, faster methods already existed. Schönhage obtained linear-time multiplication on a different machine model. Groff beat log n on a machine that can jump anywhere in memory instantly, after setup work not counted. Neither result settles the tape model.

This paper claims to prove that one fixed tape machine beats n log n. It multiplies exactly, for every input length. Its time grows like n times (log n) to the power 1 − κ, where κ = 2^−182. That is n log n divided by (log n)^κ. As n grows, this divisor grows without limit. So the ratio to n log n shrinks toward zero. If the proof holds, the n log n conjecture fails in this model.

The saving is real but extremely slow. κ is about 1.6 × 10^−55. Take n = 2^64 bits, so log n is 64. Then the cost falls short of n log n by a fraction of about 7 × 10^−55. Halving the cost would need log n near 2 to the power 2^182. The paper says its constants are extremely large. It calls the algorithm a way to establish a bound, not a practical method.

Why was n log n such a firm wall? Fast methods turn multiplication into Fourier transforms (a standard way to mix data in about log n stages). A tape machine must scan its data in order, like a cassette. Scanning n bits at each of log n stages already costs n log n. So any saving must cut both data movement and arithmetic at once.

The paper builds two new tape procedures for this. One swaps blocks of the data's address labels. Midway it stores mixed combinations of the data, not plain copies, yet the end result is an exact rearrangement. The other performs many arithmetic stages together. Both rest on a small fixed network that needs fewer smaller calls than a direct approach. Used again and again inside itself, that small surplus becomes the saving κ.

The same speed carries over to related tasks. The paper also claims division with remainder and integer square roots in the same time. It also claims faster transposing of a square grid of bits. That transposition result does not apply to models that may only move data around.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this paper, so no computer proof checker has checked it. No specialist review has been published yet.
hypeCheck: Major in theory if the proof holds, and of no practical use. The speed-up is a factor of (log n) to the power 2^−182, with extremely large constants. No Lean formalization is listed, and specialists have not yet published a review.
